content: Pentamidine has the potential to cause either hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, which may subsequently be followed by the opposite effect. When used in combination with insulin (including isophane human insulin, regular human insulin, insulin lispro, or insulin lispro protamine), the interaction mechanism is unspecified. However, caution is advised, and close monitoring of blood glucose levels is recommended. Adjustments to insulin dosage may be necessary. Pentamidine, when co-administered with ioversol, increases the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Similarly, pentamidine can elevate the levels or effects of isavuconazonium sulfate and ivacaftor by altering hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised in these cases. Pentamidine can increase the levels or effects of lemborexant by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. A lower nightly dose of lemborexant is recommended when co-administered with weak CYP3A4 inhibitors. Refer to the drug monograph for specific dosage adjustments. Both pentamidine and lenvatinib can prolong the QTc interval. Close ECG monitoring is recommended when these drugs are used together, as lenvatinib prescribing information advises caution with QT-prolonging agents. Similarly, leuprolide increases pentamidine toxicity via QTc prolongation, raising the risk of torsades de pointes. Pentamidine increases lomitapide levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The lomitapide dose should not exceed 30 mg/day. Additionally, pentamidine interacts with lumacaftor/ivacaftor by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Lumacaftor may induce, while ivacaftor may inhibit, CYP2C19 substrates. Caution and monitoring are advised. Pentamidine increases mavacamten levels by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Initiation of weak CYP2C19 inhibitors may require a reduced mavacamten dose. Similarly, pentamidine and mavorixafor both prolong the QTc interval, necessitating close monitoring of QTc in patients with risk factors for QT prolongation. Dose reduction or discontinuation of mavorixafor may be required. Pentamidine reduces the effects of metformin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Additionally, pentamidine increases the levels of intranasal midazolam by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially prolonging sedation. Caution is recommended when co-administering mild CYP3A4 inhibitors with midazolam. Pentamidine and mifepristone both prolong the QTc interval. Alternative therapies should be considered if available. Similarly, pentamidine and neomycin (oral) increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity, requiring close monitoring. Pentamidine and olodaterol (inhaled) both prolong the QTc interval, increasing the risk of ventricular arrhythmias. Caution and monitoring are advised. Pentamidine also interacts with osilodrostat and osimertinib, both of which prolong the QTc interval. Periodic ECG and electrolyte monitoring are recommended. Pentamidine and oxaliplatin increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. ECG monitoring is advised if therapy is initiated with drugs known to prolong the QT interval. Similarly, pentamidine and ozanimod both prolong the QTc interval, and treatment with ozanimod should generally not be initiated in patients concurrently treated with QT-prolonging drugs. Pentamidine and pasireotide both prolong the QTc interval, necessitating close monitoring. Pazopanib and pentamidine also prolong the QTc interval, requiring similar precautions. Pentamidine increases peramivir levels by reducing renal clearance, and caution is advised when co-administering nephrotoxic drugs. Pentamidine and potassium citrate/citric acid both increase serum potassium levels, requiring caution and monitoring. Pentamidine and quetiapine both prolong the QTc interval, and their concurrent use should be avoided in patients with risk factors for QT prolongation. Postmarketing cases have reported QT prolongation with quetiapine overdose in patients with concomitant illness or drugs causing electrolyte imbalance. Pentamidine and quinine both prolong the QTc interval, necessitating caution and monitoring. Pentamidine increases the effects of quizartinib by prolonging the QTc interval, requiring frequent ECG monitoring. Rilpivirine increases pentamidine toxicity via QTc prolongation, and caution is advised when co-administering drugs with a known risk of torsades de pointes. Pentamidine increases rucaparib levels by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Dosage adjustments of CYP2C19 substrates may be necessary. Selpercatinib increases pentamidine toxicity via QTc prolongation, requiring caution and monitoring. Pentamidine reduces the effects of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering metabolism. Co-administration with antibiotics decreases efficacy by altering colonic bacterial flora needed for drug activation. Sorafenib and pentamidine both prolong the QTc interval, necessitating caution and monitoring. Sparsentan increases pentamidine levels by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Stiripentol increases pentamidine levels by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Dose reduction of CYP2C19 substrates may be necessary if adverse reactions occur. Pentamidine and streptozocin increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity, requiring caution and monitoring. Similarly, pentamidine and tacrolimus increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Pentamidine increases tazemetostat levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating caution and monitoring. Tecovirimat increases pentamidine levels by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Tecovirimat is a weak inhibitor of CYP2C8 and CYP2C19. Adverse effects should be monitored when co-administered with sensitive substrates of these enzymes. Pentamidine and teicoplanin increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Similarly, pentamidine and tenofovir DF increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity, and the combination may also increase tenofovir levels. Pentamidine increases tinidazole levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Pentamidine and tipranavir both prolong the QTc interval, increasing the risk of PR or QT prolongation and cardiac arrhythmias. Triclabendazole and pentamidine both prolong the QTc interval, and triclabendazole increases pentamidine levels by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Pentamidine and trimethoprim both increase serum potassium levels. Trimethoprim decreases urinary potassium excretion, potentially causing hyperkalemia, particularly with high doses, renal insufficiency, or other hyperkalemia-inducing drugs. Triptorelin increases pentamidine toxicity via QTc prolongation, raising the risk of torsades de pointes. Pentamidine and valbenazine both prolong the QTc interval, requiring caution and monitoring. Voclosporin and pentamidine both increase serum potassium levels and prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration with nephrotoxic drugs may increase the risk of acute and/or chronic nephrotoxicity. Pentamidine and acyclovir increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Similarly, pentamidine and adefovir increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Capreomycin and pentamidine also increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Pentamidine decreases folic acid levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption, applicable only to the oral form of both agents. Foscarnet and pentamidine increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity, with a risk of severe hypocalcemia. Ganciclovir increases pentamidine toxicity via pharmacodynamic synergism. Gentamicin and pentamidine increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Pentamidine decreases L-methylfolate levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption, applicable only to the oral form of both agents. Methoxyflurane and pentamidine increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Paromomycin and pentamidine increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Similarly, pentamidine and polymyxin B increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Pentamidine increases ruxolitinib levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Streptomycin and pentamidine increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Tobramycin and pentamidine also increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Valganciclovir increases pentamidine toxicity via pharmacodynamic synergism. Vancomycin and pentamidine increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Zidovudine increases pentamidine toxicity via pharmacodynamic synergism.
